points: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) formed from ancient organisms over millions of years, so they are non-renewable. Biofuels come from recently grown biomass and are renewable.

Bioethanol: yeast ferments glucose, \(\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}\text{(aq)}  \to  2 \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{C}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}\). Biodiesel: transesterification of a triglyceride with methanol (KOH or NaOH catalyst) gives methyl esters and glycerol.
Biogas, mostly \(\text{C}\text{H}_{4}\), forms when bacteria break down organic waste without oxygen (anaerobic digestion).
Biofuels are close to carbon neutral because the \(\text{C}\text{O}_{2}\) released on burning was absorbed by the plants as they grew.

example.question: Explain why bioethanol from sugar cane is renewable but not completely carbon neutral.
steps: Sugar cane regrows within a season, so the fuel source is renewable.
The \(\text{C}\text{O}_{2}\) released when ethanol burns was taken in by the cane during photosynthesis, which offsets the emissions.
But fossil fuels are burnt to run farm machinery, make fertiliser, and transport and distil the ethanol.
example.answer: Net emissions are lower than for petrol, but the fossil energy inputs mean the cycle is not fully carbon neutral.

chem-1-1.watch: Do not say biofuels are carbon neutral without qualification. Fossil energy used in production adds net emissions.

points: Complete combustion (excess oxygen) of a hydrocarbon gives only \(\text{C}\text{O}_{2}\) and \(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\). Limited oxygen gives incomplete combustion: \(\text{C}\text{O}\) and/or soot (C) as well as water.
A thermochemical equation is balanced, has states, and shows \(\Delta  \text{H}\) for the amounts as written. Combustion is exothermic, so \(\Delta  \text{H}\) is negative.
Molar heat of combustion is the energy released when 1 mol of fuel burns completely at SLC (25 °C, 100 kPa). Water is liquid at SLC.
Doubling the equation doubles \(\Delta  \text{H}\). Reversing it changes the sign.

example.question: Write the thermochemical equation for complete combustion of propane (molar heat of combustion 2220 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)), then rewrite it for 2 mol of propane.
steps: Balance C then H then O: \(\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}\text{(g)} + 5 \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  3 \text{C}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 4 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\).
Oxygen check: 10 on the left, 6 + 4 = 10 on the right.
Add \(\Delta  \text{H}\) = −2220 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) (exothermic, so negative).

For 2 mol, double everything: \(2 \text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}\text{(g)} + 10 \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  6 \text{C}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 8 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\), \(\Delta  \text{H}\) = −4440 kJ.
example.answer: \(\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}\text{(g)} + 5 \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  3 \text{C}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 4 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\), \(\Delta  \text{H}\) = −2220 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

chem-1-2.watch: Leaving out states or writing a positive \(\Delta  \text{H}\) for combustion. Also check you used H2O(l), not H2O(g), at SLC.

points: Moles from mass: \(n = \frac{m}{M}\). Energy released = \(n \times |\Delta_c H|\).
Energy per gram (specific energy) = \(\frac{|\Delta_c H|}{M}\), giving \(\text{kJ g}^{-1}\). Fuels are compared per gram or per mole.
Convert units carefully: 1 MJ = 1000 kJ and 1 kg = 1000 g.
Give answers to the same significant figures as the data, usually three, with units.

example.question: Methanol has a molar heat of combustion of 726 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(M = 32.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\). How much energy is released by burning 10.0 g?
steps: Round to three significant figures.
example.answer: 227 kJ released

chem-1-3.watch: Using mass directly in energy = mass × \(\Delta H\). You must convert to moles first.

points: Energy absorbed by water: \(q = mc\Delta T\), with \(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\). Use the mass of the water (1 mL = 1 g), not the fuel.
A calorimeter is calibrated with a heater: \(E = VIt\) (time in seconds), then calibration factor \(= \frac{E}{\Delta T}\) in \(\text{J }{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\).
Reaction energy = calibration factor × \(\Delta T\). Then \(\Delta H = \frac{q}{n}\), per mole of fuel.
Heat losses to the surroundings make a measured molar enthalpy smaller than the data-book value.

example.question: Burning 1.15 g of ethanol (\(M = 46.0\)) raises the temperature of 200 g of water by 40.0 °C. Calculate the experimental molar heat of combustion.
steps: \(q = mc\Delta T = 200 \times 4.18 \times 40.0 = 33\,440\ \text{J} = 33.4\ \text{kJ}\).
example.answer: About 1.34 × 10³ \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), a bit below the data-book 1364 because of heat loss.

chem-1-4.watch: Using the mass of fuel in \(mc\Delta T\), or leaving minutes unconverted in \(VIt\). Time must be in seconds.

points: The electrochemical series ranks half-equations by \(E^\circ\) (volts, SLC, 1 M). Oxidising agents are on the left, reducing agents on the right.
The strongest oxidising agent has the most positive \(E^\circ\). The strongest reducing agent has the most negative \(E^\circ\).
A reaction is predicted when the oxidising agent is higher (more positive \(E^\circ\)) than the reducing agent's half-equation.
Metals below \(\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_{2}\) (\(E^\circ = 0.00\) V) react with dilute acid to give hydrogen gas.

example.question: Will copper metal react with 1.0 M silver nitrate solution?
steps: \(\text{Ag}^{+} + e^{-}  \to  \text{Ag}\) has \(E^\circ = +0.80\) V; \(\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2 e^{-}  \to  \text{Cu}\) has \(E^\circ = +0.34\) V.
\(\text{Ag}^{+}\) is the stronger oxidising agent, and \(\text{Cu}\) is the reducing agent, so it is predicted to react.
Reaction: \(2 \text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu}\text{(s)}  \to  2 \text{Ag}\text{(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\).
example.answer: Yes, silver forms on the copper and the solution turns blue.

chem-2-1.watch: The series predicts only whether a reaction can happen, not how fast. A predicted reaction may be too slow to see.

points: Galvanic cells turn chemical energy into electrical energy by a spontaneous redox reaction. Oxidation at the anode (negative), reduction at the cathode (positive).
Electrons flow anode to cathode through the external wire. In the salt bridge, anions move toward the anode and cations toward the cathode.
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\). A positive value means the cell reaction is spontaneous.
Balance electrons by multiplying half-equations, but never multiply \(E^\circ\).

example.question: A galvanic cell has a Zn/\(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) half-cell (\(-0.76\) V) and an Ag/\(\text{Ag}^{+}\) half-cell (+0.80 V). Find the cathode, overall equation and \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\).
steps: Higher \(E^\circ\): silver is reduced, so Ag is the cathode and Zn is the anode.
Anode: \(\text{Zn}\text{(s)}  \to  \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\). Cathode (multiplied by 2): \(\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + e^{-}  \to  \text{Ag}\text{(s)}\).
Overall: \(\text{Zn}\text{(s)} + 2 \text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)}  \to  \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{Ag}\text{(s)}\).
example.answer: Cathode Ag; overall \(\text{Zn}\text{(s)} + 2 \text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)}  \to  \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{Ag}\text{(s)}\); 1.56 V.

chem-2-2.watch: Doubling the silver half-equation does not double its \(E^\circ\). Voltage is not multiplied by coefficients.

points: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell with reactants (fuel and oxygen) supplied continuously from outside, so it does not go flat while supplied.

Acidic hydrogen cell: anode \(\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  2 \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\); cathode \(\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 4 \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4 e^{-}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\).

Alkaline hydrogen cell: anode \(\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 2 e^{-}\); cathode \(\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 4 e^{-}  \to  4 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}\).

Electrodes are porous and coated with a catalyst, giving a large surface area and faster reactions. Overall: \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\).

example.question: Write the overall equation for an alkaline hydrogen fuel cell from its half-equations.
steps: Anode: \(\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 2 e^{-}\), multiplied by 2 gives \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + 4 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}  \to  4 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 4 e^{-}\).
Cathode: \(\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 4 e^{-}  \to  4 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}\).
Add: 4 electrons cancel, 4 \(\text{O}\text{H}^{-}\) cancel, and 2 \(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\) cancel from the right.
example.answer: \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\), the same overall reaction as in an acidic cell.

chem-2-3.watch: Matching the half-equation to the electrolyte. Do not use \(\text{H}^{+}\) in an alkaline cell or \(\text{O}\text{H}^{-}\) in an acidic cell.

points: Green hydrogen is made by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity: \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}  \to  2 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}\). It has no carbon emissions in production.

Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas by steam reforming, \(\text{C}\text{H}_{4}\text{(g)} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(g)}  \to  \text{C}\text{O}\text{(g)} + 3 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)}\), and releases \(\text{C}\text{O}_{2}\). Blue hydrogen is the same, but captures the \(\text{C}\text{O}_{2}\).
The hydrogen itself is identical in each case. The colour describes how it was made.
Challenges: cost, large renewable electricity demand, and storing and transporting a low-density gas.

example.question: What mass of hydrogen can be made by electrolysing 1.00 kg of water? Use \(M(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 18.0\) and \(M(\text{H}_2) = 2.02\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\).
steps: The ratio \(\text{H}_{2}\text{O} : \text{H}_{2}\) is 2 : 2, so \(n(\text{H}_2) = 55.6\ \text{mol}\).
example.answer: About 112 g of hydrogen

chem-2-4.watch: Calling hydrogen green because it burns cleanly. Green depends on how it is made, using renewable electricity.

points: Collision theory: reactant particles must collide with energy at least the activation energy (\(E_a\)) and with the correct orientation. Only these are successful collisions.
Higher concentration, pressure (gases) or surface area means more frequent collisions, so a faster rate.
Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so collisions are more frequent and a greater proportion are successful. The proportion effect is the main one.
Rate = change in concentration or mass per unit time. A catalyst lowers \(E_a\).

example.question: Explain, using collision theory, why zinc powder reacts faster than zinc granules with the same acid.
steps: Powder has a much larger surface area exposed to the acid.
More zinc atoms can be hit by \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions at once, so collisions per second increase.
The energy and \(E_a\) are unchanged, so the proportion of successful collisions is the same, but the number per second is greater.
example.answer: The greater collision frequency gives a faster rate. The total amount of product is unchanged.

chem-3-1.watch: Saying higher concentration increases the energy of particles. It only increases how often they collide.

points: A Maxwell–Boltzmann curve plots number of particles against kinetic energy. The area under the curve is the total number of particles.
At higher temperature the peak moves right and gets lower and broader. The area is the same, but more particles are beyond \(E_a\).
A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower \(E_a\). The curve does not change, but the \(E_a\) line moves left, so more particles can react.
A catalyst is not consumed and does not change \(\Delta H\) or the equilibrium position.

example.question: Use a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution to explain how a catalyst increases reaction rate.
steps: The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
On the curve, the \(E_a\) line moves to the left.
The area to the right of the line is larger, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful, and the rate increases.
example.answer: More particles have energy at least \(E_a\), giving more successful collisions per second, at the same temperature.

chem-3-2.watch: Do not shift the whole curve for a catalyst. Only temperature changes the curve; a catalyst moves the \(E_a\) line.

points: Kc = [products] raised to coefficients ÷ [reactants] raised to coefficients, at equilibrium. Include gases and aqueous species only; leave out solids and liquids.
Units come from the expression. For \(\text{N}_{2}\text{(g)} + 3 \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)}  \rightleftharpoons  2 \text{N}\text{H}_{3}\text{(g)}\), \(K_c\) has units \(\text{M}^{-2}\).
Reverse the equation: \(K' = \frac{1}{K}\). Multiply coefficients by \(n\): \(K' = K^n\).
Kc depends only on temperature. Compare \(Q\) with \(K\): if \(Q < K\), the reaction goes forward.

example.question: 1.00 mol of \(\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}\) is placed in a 2.00 L vessel. At equilibrium \(\text{N}\text{O}_{2}\) is 0.200 M. Find \(K_c\) for \(\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}\text{(g)}  \rightleftharpoons  2 \text{N}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}\).
steps: \(\text{N}\text{O}_{2}\) is 0.200 M, so \(\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}\) used = 0.100 M and \([\text{N}_2\text{O}_4] = 0.400\ \text{M}\).

chem-3-3.watch: Changing concentration, pressure or adding a catalyst does not change K. Only a temperature change does.

points: Le Chatelier: if an equilibrium is disturbed, the system shifts to partly oppose the change.
Adding reactant shifts right. Increasing pressure (smaller volume) favours the side with fewer gas moles. Adding water dilutes and favours the side with more particles.
Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction and changes K. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not change yield or K.
Industry compromises: a moderate temperature gives acceptable yield at an economical rate.

example.question: For \(2 \text{S}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}  \rightleftharpoons  2 \text{S}\text{O}_{3}\text{(g)}\), \(\Delta  \text{H}\) = −198 kJ. How does decreasing temperature affect rate, yield and K?
steps: The forward reaction is exothermic.
Lower temperature favours the exothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts right: yield of \(\text{S}\text{O}_{3}\) and K increase.
Lower temperature also lowers the collision energy, so the rate decreases.
example.answer: Yield and K go up, but the reaction is slower. This is why a compromise temperature is used.

chem-3-4.watch: Saying a catalyst increases yield. It only helps the system reach equilibrium sooner.

points: Electrolytic cells use an external power supply to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. Oxidation at the anode (positive), reduction at the cathode (negative).
Molten salts contain only their own ions: for example, molten NaCl gives Na(l) at the cathode and \(\text{Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}\) at the anode.
In aqueous solution, water competes. Ions of reactive metals such as \(\text{K}^{+}\) and \(\text{Na}^{+}\) are not reduced; water is reduced to \(\text{H}_{2}\) and \(\text{O}\text{H}^{-}\) instead.
At the anode, the strongest reductant is oxidised: a halide or water with inert electrodes.

example.question: Predict the products when 1 M KI(aq) is electrolysed with graphite electrodes.
steps: Cathode: \(\text{K}^{+}\) cannot be reduced in water, so \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 2 e^{-}  \to  \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}\) (\(-0.83\) V).
Anode: \(\text{I}^{-}\) (+0.54 V) is a stronger reductant than water (+1.23 V): \(2 \text{I}^{-}\text{(aq)}  \to  \text{I}_{2}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\).

Overall: \(2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)} + 2 \text{I}^{-}\text{(aq)}  \to  \text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{I}_{2}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{O}\text{H}^{-}\text{(aq)}\), needing more than \(0.54 - (-0.83) = 1.37\) V.
example.answer: \(\text{H}_{2}\) at the cathode and \(\text{I}_{2}\) at the anode.

chem-4-1.watch: Writing \(\text{K}^{+}  \to  \text{K}\) or \(\text{Na}^{+}  \to  \text{Na}\) in aqueous solution. Water is reduced instead.

points: Charge: \(Q = It\), with current in amps and time in seconds. Moles of electrons: \(n(e^-) = \frac{Q}{F}\), where \(F = 96\,500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}\).
Use the half-equation ratio to get moles of product, then \(m = nM\). Gas volume at SLC: \(V = n \times 24.8\ \text{L}\).
Cells in series carry the same charge, so the same number of moles of electrons.
Plan: \(I,t \to Q \to n(e^-) \to n(\text{product}) \to m\).

example.question: A current of 3.00 A flows for 20.0 minutes through \(\text{Ag}\text{N}\text{O}_{3}\text{(aq)}\). What mass of silver is deposited?
steps: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + e^{-}  \to  \text{Ag}\text{(s)}\): ratio 1 : 1, so \(n(\text{Ag}) = 0.0373\ \text{mol}\).
example.answer: 4.03 g of silver

chem-4-2.watch: Using minutes in \(Q = It\). Always convert to seconds first.

points: Secondary cells are rechargeable. Discharging is a galvanic cell. Recharging is an electrolytic cell driven by an external supply.
They work because the discharge products stay on the electrodes, so the reverse reaction can regenerate the reactants.
On recharge, connect positive to positive and negative to negative. The anode and cathode roles swap, but each electrode keeps its + or − sign.

Lead–acid discharge overall: \(\text{Pb}\text{(s)} + \text{Pb}\text{O}_{2}\text{(s)} + 4 \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{S}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)}  \to  2 \text{Pb}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}\).

example.question: Write the half-equation at the negative electrode and the overall reaction when a lead–acid battery is recharged.
steps: At the negative electrode, \(\text{Pb}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\) is reduced back to lead: \(\text{Pb}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2 e^{-}  \to  \text{Pb}\text{(s)} + \text{S}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)}\).

At the positive electrode: \(\text{Pb}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}  \to  \text{Pb}\text{O}_{2}\text{(s)} + 4 \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{S}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\).

Add: \(2 \text{Pb}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2 \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{(l)}  \to  \text{Pb}\text{(s)} + \text{Pb}\text{O}_{2}\text{(s)} + 4 \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2 \text{S}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)}\).
example.answer: The overall equation is the reverse of discharge, and the sulfuric acid concentration increases.

chem-4-3.watch: Thinking the negative electrode becomes the anode on recharge. It stays negative, but it is now the cathode.

points: Electroplating: the object to be plated is the cathode (negative). The plating metal is usually the anode (positive). The electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal.

Cathode: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}  \to  \text{Cu}\text{(s)}\). Anode: \(\text{Cu}\text{(s)}  \to  \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\). The electrolyte concentration stays roughly constant.
Galvanic cells are spontaneous with a negative anode. Electrolytic cells need a power supply and have a positive anode.
In both types, oxidation is at the anode, reduction at the cathode, and electrons move anode to cathode through the wire.

example.question: Describe how to copper-plate a steel key, and find the mass deposited by 2.00 A for 965 s.
steps: Key is the cathode (negative); copper is the anode (positive); electrolyte is \(\text{Cu}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\text{(aq)}\).
Cathode: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}  \to  \text{Cu}\text{(s)}\). Anode: \(\text{Cu}\text{(s)}  \to  \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2 e^{-}\).
example.answer: 0.635 g of copper deposits on the key (the cathode).

chem-4-4.watch: Putting the object on the anode. The object being plated is always the cathode.

points: Prefixes for chain length: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-. Find the longest carbon chain containing the main functional group.
Suffixes: -ane (alkane), -ene (alkene), -anol (alcohol), -anal (aldehyde), -anone (ketone), -anoic acid, -anamine, -anamide. Esters: alkyl alkanoate.
Number the chain so the main functional group gets the lowest number, then name side groups in alphabetical order with their numbers.
Haloalkanes use prefixes such as chloro- and bromo-, for example 2-chloropropane.

example.question: Name \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{H}(\text{C}\text{H}_{3})\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{H}\).
steps: The longest chain containing the carbon with –OH has four carbons: butane.
Number from the –OH end so it gets 1: butan-1-ol.
The methyl group is on carbon 3 (counting from the –OH end).
example.answer: 3-methylbutan-1-ol

chem-5-1.watch: Numbering from the end nearest a side group instead of the functional group. The functional group gets the lowest number.

points: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different bonding arrangements: chain, position or functional group isomers.
Cis–trans (geometric) isomers need a C=C with two different groups on each carbon. Cis has similar groups on the same side.
Optical isomers (enantiomers) arise from a chiral carbon, one bonded to four different groups. They are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
To count isomers, systematically shorten the main chain, then move branches and functional groups.

example.question: How many alcohol structural isomers have the formula \(\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{O}\text{H}\), and which is chiral?
steps: Four-carbon chain: butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.
Three-carbon chain with a methyl: 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Butan-2-ol has carbon 2 bonded to –H, –OH, –\(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\) and –\(\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\), four different groups.
example.answer: 4 isomers; butan-2-ol is chiral.

chem-5-2.watch: Counting a drawing that is rotated or flipped as a new isomer. Check whether the atom connections have actually changed.

points: Addition: an alkene adds \(\text{H}_{2}\) (Ni or Pt), \(\text{Br}_{2}\), HX or \(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\) (steam, \(\text{H}_{3}\text{P}\text{O}_{4}\)) across C=C to give a saturated product.
Substitution: an alkane reacts with \(\text{Cl}_{2}\) in UV light, replacing H with Cl. A haloalkane reacts with \(\text{O}\text{H}^{-}\) to give an alcohol.

Oxidation: primary alcohol to aldehyde to carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol to ketone; tertiary alcohols do not oxidise. Reagents: acidified \(\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}\) (orange to green) or acidified \(\text{Mn}\text{O}_{4}^{-}\).
Condensation joins two molecules and releases water (esters, amides). Hydrolysis splits a molecule using water.

example.question: What is formed when propan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate, and what is the colour change?
steps: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol (OH on a carbon bonded to two other carbons).
Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones. Oxidation stops there.
\(\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}\) is reduced to \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\).
example.answer: Propanone is formed; orange to green.

chem-5-3.watch: Thinking all alcohols oxidise to acids. Secondary give ketones and tertiary do not react.

points: Reaction pathways link families: alkene to alkane (\(\text{H}_{2}\)), alkanol (\(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\)) or haloalkane (HX); haloalkane to alkanol (\(\text{O}\text{H}^{-}\)) or amine (\(\text{N}\text{H}_{3}\)); alkanol to alkanoic acid by oxidation.
Esterification: carboxylic acid + alkanol \( \rightleftharpoons \) ester + water, with concentrated \(\text{H}_{2}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\) catalyst and heat. It is reversible, so yield is below 100%.
Name an ester as alkyl (from the alcohol) then alkanoate (from the acid): methanol and butanoic acid give methyl butanoate.
Overall yield for a multi-step pathway is the product of the step yields.

example.question: Outline a three-step pathway from ethene to ethyl ethanoate.
steps: Step 1: hydration with steam, \(\text{H}_{3}\text{P}\text{O}_{4}\) catalyst: ethene gives ethanol.
Step 2: oxidise some ethanol by heating under reflux with acidified \(\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}\) to give ethanoic acid.

Step 3: warm ethanol and ethanoic acid with concentrated \(\text{H}_{2}\text{S}\text{O}_{4}\): \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\text{O}\text{H} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}  \rightleftharpoons  \text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\text{O}\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\).
example.answer: Ethyl ethanoate is made from ethanol (the ethyl part) and ethanoic acid.

chem-5-4.watch: Swapping the parent molecules in the name. The alcohol supplies the alkyl group, and the acid supplies the -oate part.

points: Intermolecular forces in order of strength: dispersion (all molecules, stronger with larger size and surface contact), dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding (O–H or N–H).
For similar molar mass, boiling point rises: alkane, then ester/aldehyde/ketone, then alcohol, then carboxylic acid. Branching lowers boiling point.
Small alcohols, acids and amines dissolve in water through hydrogen bonding. Solubility falls as the non-polar chain gets longer.
Boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

example.question: Rank butane, propanone, propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid (all about 58–60 \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\)) by boiling point and explain.
steps: Butane is non-polar, so only dispersion forces: lowest.
Propanone is polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces as well.
Propan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding through its –OH.
Ethanoic acid forms stronger hydrogen-bonded pairs (dimers): highest.
example.answer: Butane < propanone < propan-1-ol < ethanoic acid.

chem-5-5.watch: Saying covalent bonds break on boiling. Compare intermolecular forces, not bond strengths.

points: In mass spectrometry the molecule is ionised, fragmented, and the positive ions are separated by mass-to-charge ratio, \(m/z\).
The molecular ion peak \(\text{M}^{+}\) has \(m/z\) equal to the molar mass. The base peak is the tallest peak (100%) and is not always \(\text{M}^{+}\).
Fragment ion peaks are found by subtracting from M, for example 15 for \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\) and 29 for \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\). Compare with the data book.
Chlorine gives M and M+2 peaks in a 3 : 1 ratio. Bromine gives M and M+2 peaks about 1 : 1.

example.question: Ethanol has a molecular ion peak at \(m/z = 46\) and peaks at 31 and 29. Assign them.
steps: \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}\): \(2 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 + 16 = 46\), so the peak at 46 is \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}^{+}\).
example.answer: 46 is \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}^{+}\), 31 is \(\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\text{H}^{+}\) and 29 is \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}\).

chem-6-1.watch: Forgetting the + charge on fragments, or assuming the tallest peak is the molecular ion.

points: IR spectroscopy shows which bonds are present. A bond absorbs when its vibration changes the dipole moment. The axis is wavenumber in \(\text{cm}^{-1}\).
Key absorptions: alcohol O–H 3200–3550 (broad); acid O–H 2500–3000 (very broad); C=O 1670–1750 (strong); N–H 3300–3500.
Check for what is absent as well as present. No C=O means no aldehyde, ketone, acid or ester.
The fingerprint region, below about 1500 \(\text{cm}^{-1}\), is unique to each compound.

example.question: A compound \(\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2}\) shows a strong peak near 1710 \(\text{cm}^{-1}\) and a very broad band from 2500 to 3000 \(\text{cm}^{-1}\). Is it propanoic acid or methyl ethanoate?
steps: The 1710 peak shows a C=O bond. Both candidates have it.
The very broad band at 2500–3000 is an O–H in a carboxylic acid.
Methyl ethanoate has no O–H bond.
example.answer: Propanoic acid

chem-6-2.watch: Using one peak alone. C=O at about 1700 appears in several families, so check for O–H and other bonds.

points: \(^{1}\text{H}\) NMR: the number of signals equals the number of different hydrogen environments. Chemical shift (ppm) is measured from TMS at 0 ppm.
Peak area (integration) gives the ratio of hydrogens in each environment.
Splitting (high resolution): \(n\) hydrogens on neighbouring carbons give \(n + 1\) peaks (singlet, doublet, triplet, quartet).
\(^{13}\text{C}\) NMR: one signal for each different carbon environment. Symmetry makes some carbons equivalent.

example.question: Predict the \(^{1}\text{H}\) and \(^{13}\text{C}\) NMR spectra for ethyl ethanoate, \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\text{O}\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\).
steps: \(^{1}\text{H}\): three environments, so three signals: \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\) (3H, singlet, about 2 ppm), \(\text{O}\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\) (2H, quartet, about 4 ppm), \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\) (3H, triplet, about 1 ppm).
Splitting: \(\text{O}\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\) has 3 neighbouring H (quartet); \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\) has 2 (triplet); \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\) has none (singlet).
\(^{13}\text{C}\): four different carbons (C=O, \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\text{C}\text{O}\), \(\text{O}\text{C}\text{H}_{2}\), \(\text{C}\text{H}_{3}\)), so four signals.
example.answer: 3 signals in \(^{1}\text{H}\) (3 : 2 : 3 area ratio) and 4 signals in \(^{13}\text{C}\).

chem-6-3.watch: Counting hydrogens on the same carbon for splitting. Splitting depends only on hydrogens on adjacent carbons.

points: HPLC separates a mixture: a liquid mobile phase carries it through a column. Components held more strongly by the stationary phase have longer retention times.
Reversed-phase: non-polar stationary phase, polar mobile phase, so the most polar component elutes first.
Quantitative HPLC: peak area compared to a calibration curve of standards of known concentration.
Titration: \(n = cV\) (V in L). Use the average of concordant titres (within 0.10 mL) and the mole ratio from the balanced equation.

example.question: 20.00 mL of NaOH solution is neutralised by 18.50 mL of 0.100 M HCl. Find \(c(\text{NaOH})\).
steps: \(\text{H}\text{Cl} + \text{Na}\text{O}\text{H}  \to  \text{Na}\text{Cl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}\): ratio 1 : 1.
\(n(\text{HCl}) = 0.100 \times 0.01850 = 1.850 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\), so \(n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.850 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\).
example.answer: \(c(\text{NaOH}) = 0.0925\ \text{M}\)

chem-6-4.watch: Leaving volumes in mL when using \(n = cV\). Convert to litres.

points: A 2-amino acid has an amino group (–\(\text{N}\text{H}_{2}\)) and carboxyl group (–COOH) on the same carbon, plus a side chain R that differs between amino acids.
Amino acids join by condensation, losing water to form a peptide (amide) bond. A chain of \(n\) residues has \(n - 1\) peptide bonds.
Protein structure: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix and β-pleated sheet, hydrogen bonds in the backbone), tertiary (3D fold from R-group interactions).
Heat or pH changes break the weak interactions and denature the protein. Peptide bonds stay intact.

example.question: Glycine (75.0) and alanine (89.0 \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\)) form a dipeptide. What is its molar mass?
steps: One condensation reaction, so one water (18.0) is lost.

chem-7-1.watch: Subtracting 18.0 for every amino acid. Subtract 18.0 once per peptide bond, which is one fewer than the residues.

points: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose, \(\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}\)) join by condensation into disaccharides: sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose.
Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) are long chains of glucose units. Hydrolysis breaks them back down.
A triglyceride is glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds. Hydrolysis gives glycerol and three fatty acids.
Saturated fats pack tightly, so they are solid. Unsaturated oils have C=C kinks that weaken dispersion forces, so they are liquid at room temperature.

example.question: Explain why olive oil is liquid at room temperature but beef fat is solid.
steps: Olive oil is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, which contain C=C double bonds.
The double bonds bend the chains, so molecules cannot pack closely, giving weaker dispersion forces.
Beef fat is mostly saturated, with straight chains packing tightly and stronger dispersion forces.
example.answer: Weaker forces between oil molecules give a lower melting point, so olive oil is liquid.

chem-7-2.watch: Mixing up the reactions. Condensation joins molecules and releases water; hydrolysis splits them using water.

points: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy by providing an alternative pathway. They are specific to their substrate and are not consumed.
The substrate binds at the active site. Induced fit says the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds.
Enzymes have an optimum temperature and pH. Extremes break weak interactions, changing the active site shape (denaturation).
Vitamins: water-soluble (B group, C) are needed regularly. Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) can be stored. Some vitamins act as coenzymes.

example.question: An enzyme works best at 37 °C. Explain what happens to the rate of reaction at 70 °C.
steps: Higher temperature first increases collisions, but 70 °C is well above the optimum.
The weak bonds holding the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape.
The substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is denatured.
example.answer: The rate drops sharply, and the damage is usually irreversible.

chem-7-3.watch: Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds. It breaks weak interactions in the tertiary structure; the amino acid sequence remains.

points: Food energy values: carbohydrate 16 \(\text{kJ g}^{-1}\), protein 17 \(\text{kJ g}^{-1}\), fat 37 \(\text{kJ g}^{-1}\).
Total energy = sum of (mass × energy value) for each nutrient.
Digestion is hydrolysis: carbohydrates to glucose and other monosaccharides, proteins to amino acids, fats to glycerol and fatty acids.
Food energy can be measured in a calorimeter, using \(q = mc\Delta T\) or calibration factor × \(\Delta T\).

example.question: 100 g of a snack contains 10.0 g protein, 12.0 g fat and 50.0 g carbohydrate. Estimate the energy content.
steps: Protein: \(10.0 \times 17 = 170\ \text{kJ}\).
Fat: \(12.0 \times 37 = 444\ \text{kJ}\).
Carbohydrate: \(50.0 \times 16 = 800\ \text{kJ}\).
example.answer: About 1.41 × 10³ kJ per 100 g

chem-7-4.watch: Using one energy value for the whole mass. Multiply each nutrient's mass by its own value.

points: Green chemistry aims to reduce hazards and waste. Principles include prevention of waste, atom economy, less hazardous synthesis, safer chemicals and solvents, and energy efficiency.
More principles: renewable feedstocks, reducing derivatives, catalysis, design for degradation, real-time pollution monitoring, and accident prevention.
Prevention is better than treating waste, because treatment costs energy and money and may create more waste.
Catalysts save energy and are not consumed, so they support green chemistry.

example.question: A factory replaces a stoichiometric reagent with a recyclable catalyst. Which green chemistry principles are supported?
steps: Catalysis: the catalyst is regenerated and used in small amounts.
Prevention and atom economy: less reagent waste is produced.
Energy efficiency: a catalyst often allows lower temperatures.
example.answer: Catalysis, waste prevention and energy efficiency.

chem-8-1.watch: Saying catalysts increase yield at equilibrium. They speed up the reaction but do not change the equilibrium position.

points: Atom economy = \(\frac{M(\text{desired product}) \times \text{coefficient}}{\text{total } M \text{ of all reactants}} \times 100\), using the balanced equation.
It measures how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product. A high value means less waste.
Addition reactions that make only one product have 100% atom economy.
Atom economy is different from percentage yield. It depends only on the equation, not on what you collect.

example.question: Iron is made by \(\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}\text{(s)} + 3 \text{C}\text{O}\text{(g)}  \to  2 \text{Fe}\text{(s)} + 3 \text{C}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}\). Calculate the atom economy for iron (Fe = 55.8, O = 16.0, C = 12.0).
steps: Desired product: \(2 \times 55.8 = 111.6\).

chem-8-2.watch: Forgetting coefficients. Multiply each molar mass by its coefficient, and use reactants only in the denominator.

points: Percentage yield = \(\frac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}} \times 100\).
Theoretical yield: convert the limiting reactant to moles, use the mole ratio, then convert the product to mass.
Yield is below 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions and losses during separation and purification.
Multi-step overall yield = product of the step yields. Fewer steps usually means less waste.

example.question: 10.0 g of ethene is hydrated to ethanol: \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}  \to  \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}\text{H}\). 12.6 g of ethanol is collected. Find the percentage yield (M of ethene 28.0, ethanol 46.0 \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\)).
steps: Ratio 1 : 1, so \(n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}) = 0.357\ \text{mol}\).
Theoretical mass = \(0.357 \times 46.0 = 16.4\ \text{g}\).

chem-8-3.watch: Ignoring the mole ratio or comparing actual mass with the starting reactant mass.

points: A linear economy is take, make, use, dispose. A circular economy keeps materials in use as long as possible and designs out waste.
Strategies: reduce, reuse, repair, recycle, recover, and redesign products. Renewable energy supports circular systems.
Chemistry examples: recovering and reusing solvents, finding uses for by-products (such as glycerol from biodiesel), and recycling PET, glass and batteries.
Victoria's container deposit scheme returns bottles and cans to be reprocessed.

example.question: Explain how recycling aluminium cans is an example of a circular economy.
steps: Cans are collected and melted down rather than discarded as waste.
The recycled aluminium makes new cans, so the material stays in use.
Recycling needs far less energy than extracting aluminium from bauxite, so it also saves resources.
example.answer: Aluminium stays in a closed loop, with less waste and lower energy use than the linear model.

chem-8-4.watch: Equating recycling alone with a circular economy. Designing out waste, reuse and repair also matter.

points: Identify the type of question first: calorimetry, equilibrium, electrolysis, organic, analysis or green chemistry. Then pick the right formula or rule.
Show the unit conversions: minutes to seconds, mL to L, kJ to MJ, mass to moles.
For equilibrium, compare \(Q\) with \(K\). If \(Q < K\), the system moves forward; if \(Q > K\), it moves in reverse.
Check the answer is sensible, with correct significant figures and units.

example.question: For \(\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{I}_{2}\text{(g)}  \rightleftharpoons  2 \text{H}\text{I}\text{(g)}\), \(K = 50.0\). A mixture has \(\text{H}_{2}\) = \(\text{I}_{2}\) = 0.020 M and \(\text{H}\text{I}\) = 0.060 M. Which way does it shift?
steps: \(Q < K\), so there is too little product for equilibrium.
example.answer: It shifts forward (right), making more HI, until \(Q = 50.0\).

chem-challenge.watch: Using K instead of Q for a mixture that is not at equilibrium. Compute Q from the given concentrations.
